question: In a 1960 Montreal study, one bilingual voice read in English and in French. How did French-Canadian listeners rate the French version?
options: About the same as the English
answer: Lower than the English one. Each speaker recorded both versions, so any gap had to come from the language, not the voice. French-Canadian listeners rated the English guises better-looking, more intelligent and more dependable, and on some traits marked the French guises down further than English-Canadian listeners did.
move: A group can absorb the very ranking that places it lower.
trap: Expecting listeners to favour speakers of their own language.
source: Lambert et al., J. Abnormal Social Psychology, 1960
reference: Lambert, Hodgson, Gardner & Fillenbaum, Evaluational reactions to spoken languages, Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology 60(1), 1960
